passage: “Top of the class again!” Papa said, tapping Leela's report card. “Our Leela never lets us down.” The guests clapped. Her younger sister Rehana kept stirring her dal. “Papa, can Rehana have a sweet too?” Leela asked. “Of course, but Rehana knows she has to study more.” Later, on the stairs, Leela held out her laddu. “Half is yours.” Rehana shrugged. “Papa only says your name.” Leela's stomach twisted. “What if I get less next time? Will he stop?” “Maybe,” Rehana said. Leela looked at the card in her hand as if it had grown heavier.

qa.q: What did Rehana keep doing while the guests clapped?
qa.a: Rehana kept stirring her dal.

qa.q: What is Leela worried about when she asks, “What if I get less next time?”
qa.a: Leela is worried that Papa's praise depends on her marks and could disappear, and she feels uneasy that her sister is hurt.

qa.q: What could Papa do differently at the next report card?
qa.a: Papa could praise effort from both sisters and avoid comparing them, so Leela feels less pressure and Rehana is not left out.

qa.q: How does Rehana see the praise given to Leela?
qa.a: Rehana feels overlooked. She says, “Papa only says your name,” and shrugs it off as if she has learned not to expect more.

grounding: A openly preferred child enjoys the praise, feels uneasy about her sister's hurt and worries about having to keep earning the position.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: I'm Harish, and I was the child everybody praised. When relatives came for the weekend, Nana held up my drawing book and Mausi said, “Harish is the clever one.” My brother Pankaj went out to the terrace and threw a ball against the wall by himself. I felt proud for about a minute, then a knot in my stomach. I took him a glass of water and offered to share my sweets. “Don't bother,” he said. That night I lay awake thinking that if I stopped being clever, I would lose my place, and wondering whether Pankaj noticed how tightly I held on.

qa.q: Where did Pankaj go while the relatives praised Harish?
qa.a: Pankaj went out to the terrace and threw a ball against the wall by himself.

qa.q: Why did Harish feel a knot in the stomach after feeling proud?
qa.a: Harish seems to feel guilty about Pankaj's hurt and afraid that being less clever would cost the place. The sleepless night suggests pressure to keep earning it.

qa.q: What could Harish try the next time relatives praise only one child?
qa.a: Harish could steer the talk to something Pankaj is good at, or spend time with Pankaj afterwards and say the comparison feels unfair.

qa.q: What might Pankaj be feeling on the terrace?
qa.a: Pankaj may feel left out or hurt, which fits going off alone and saying “Don't bother” to Harish's kind offer.

grounding: A favoured child enjoys praise, feels guilt over a sibling's hurt and senses pressure to keep the position.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was the big family lunch at Nani's house. Everyone passed my drawing around. Papa said, 'Ritu got the art prize, our little star.' Chetan bhaiya came first in the chess tournament last week, but nobody asked about it. He went out to the balcony and didn't eat dessert.
I liked being the star, I really did. But my stomach felt funny when I saw his face. Nani's neighbour said, 'You must win again next year!' What if I don't? Will they stop saying star?
Tonight I went to bhaiya's room and asked him to teach me chess. He said maybe tomorrow.
Ritu

qa.q: What prize did Ritu win?
qa.a: The art prize.

qa.q: What might Ritu be worried about after the neighbour's comment?
qa.a: Ritu feels anxious about not winning again next year and losing the 'star' place in the family.

qa.q: What small step could Papa take at the next family lunch?
qa.a: Ask about Chetan's chess win too, so both children's efforts are noticed.

qa.q: How does Chetan likely experience the lunch?
qa.a: He seems hurt and overlooked; his first place in chess went unmentioned, so he went to the balcony and skipped dessert.

grounding: A child who is openly praised enjoys it but feels uneasy about a sibling's hurt and pressure to keep winning.

passage: At the temple fair in their village, Dadi bought Swati a set of glass bangles and told the stall owner, 'This one is sharp, she will be a teacher.' Aadhya, a year older, got nothing because 'she lost her last bangles.' Swati held the box tight and smiled, but then she saw Aadhya staring at the swings, pretending not to care. On the bus home, their uncle praised Swati's recitation while Aadhya looked out of the window. Swati slipped two bangles into Aadhya's palm under the dupatta. Aadhya squeezed her hand but said nothing. At home, Swati practised her recitation again before sleeping, even though she was tired.

qa.q: What did Dadi buy Swati at the fair?
qa.a: A set of glass bangles.

qa.q: Why did Swati slip two bangles into Aadhya's palm?
qa.a: Swati felt guilty and uneasy seeing Aadhya pretend not to care, and wanted to share what she had been given.

qa.q: What could Dadi do differently at the next fair?
qa.a: Get each girl something small and praise Aadhya for something real, instead of reminding her about lost bangles.

qa.q: What might Aadhya be going through on the bus home?
qa.a: Probably hurt and invisible while their uncle praised only Swati, and a little comforted when Swati quietly shared the bangles.

grounding: A favoured child enjoys a grandmother's praise, feels uneasy about her sister's hurt and keeps working to earn the praise.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Every Sunday at Grandma Ingrid's flat in Gothenburg, the talk turned to Priscila's football goals. 'Our champion!' said Grandpa, raising his coffee cup. Her brother Anders, who spent weekends building model trains, cleared the plates without being asked. Nobody noticed. Priscila liked the cheering, and her cheeks went warm. But when she saw Anders standing alone at the sink, the warm feeling turned heavy. 'Anders built a bridge that actually opens,' she said suddenly. The table went quiet. Grandpa asked, 'Does it?' and Anders turned around, surprised. Later, Priscila lay awake wondering if she had to score again next week, or if they would stop calling her champion.

qa.q: What does Anders spend his weekends doing?
qa.a: Building model trains.

qa.q: How did Priscila's feeling change when she saw Anders alone at the sink?
qa.a: Her warm, proud feeling turned heavy; she felt guilty and uneasy that he was being overlooked.

qa.q: Which choice of Priscila's worked, and why?
qa.a: Mentioning Anders's bridge out loud; it turned the table's attention to him and got Grandpa asking about it.

qa.q: If you were Anders, what would you want from the family on Sundays?
qa.a: To be asked about the model trains and noticed for helping, not just clearing plates while Priscila is cheered.

grounding: A favoured child enjoys family praise, feels uneasy about her brother being overlooked and worries about keeping her place.

passage:
At the parent-teacher meeting, the classroom was crowded with parents on small chairs. Papa beamed at Tarun's report card. "First in maths again! This one is our star," he said loudly, and nearby parents smiled.
Tarun's younger sister Simran sat on the bench by the door, her own report card rolled tight in her hand. She had come third in her class. Nobody had asked.
Tarun felt the warm weight of Papa's hand on his shoulder, and at the same time a small sick feeling. "Papa, Simran came third. In the whole class."
Papa blinked. "Oh, very good, very good," he said, and turned back to Tarun's marks.
On the way home, Tarun gave Simran the chocolate his teacher had given him. He didn't know what else to do.

qa.q: What rank did Simran come in her class?
qa.a: She came third in her class.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Tarun have with Papa's hand on his shoulder?
qa.a: Tarun felt proud and warm at the praise, but also a small sick guilt seeing Simran ignored.

qa.q: What could Papa do differently at the next meeting?
qa.a: Look at both report cards with equal interest and praise each child's own effort, instead of calling one the star.

qa.q: What was the meeting like for Simran?
qa.a: Simran felt hurt and invisible, holding her report card tight while nobody asked about her third place.

grounding: Shows an openly favoured child enjoying praise while feeling guilty about his sister's hurt.
